title: OpenAI's business model is a negative snowball: the more it burns, the more it loses
dek: A model company must burn ten times last year's training cost on the next generation, while revenue only comes back at twice last year's training cost. Add 2, subtract 10, and cash flow goes more negative every year. Only on the day it stops burning does the income statement suddenly look good.
why: A frontline Silicon Valley investor lays out the books of OpenAI, Anthropic, Robinhood and Waymo, with concrete numbers and mechanics. The second half, on where AI revenue comes from and on the bubble, is the most valuable part.
who: Investors and founders watching AI business models, US tech stocks and private-market valuations, especially anyone trying to understand how model companies burn money and where AI revenue comes from.
skip: The first 3 minutes of self-introduction and the keyword review of 2021-25 can be fast-forwarded.

points.h: Model companies are a negative snowball
points.body: Freda reduces OpenAI's business model to a minimal equation: suppose last year's training cost is 1, and revenue the next year recovers 2, but the next generation model's training cost is 10, so 2 minus 10 equals -8. This means large models are essentially a negative snowball: every year burns more cash than the year before. There are only two ways to turn positive: either next year's revenue is more than twice last year's training cost, or you stop burning on a model 10 times bigger. Anthropic CEO Dario subdivides the latter: either you hit a physical limit and can't train further, or Scaling Law slows down and it's not worth burning another 10x.

points.h: The day you stop burning is the best-looking income statement
points.body: Freda uses Netflix as an analogy: Netflix's cash flow was negative for years, also a negative snowball, worst in 2019 at negative 3 billion; in 2020 the pandemic halted content production and content costs disappeared, and cash flow suddenly turned positive to 2 billion. Model companies are the same: the thing you burn money on only truly generates cash flow on the day you stop burning it, and at that moment the income statement looks very good. Freda calls it "very violent aesthetics." But he also admits Netflix won't stop investing in content entirely, just that the growth rate comes down; model companies are the same — training costs no longer increasing several times a year is enough for margins.

points.h: The market underestimates OpenAI's enterprise side
points.body: OpenAI has four revenue lines: ChatGPT accounts for over 70% (including enterprise GPT), API, Agent (including the SoftBank partnership), and new products. The company itself predicts the latter two lines grow faster and take a larger share in the future. Freda points out a non-consensus view: everyone sees OpenAI as a pure 2C company, but today its individual and enterprise sides are roughly equal, and enterprise users already number in the millions. The enterprise side as a super entry point will develop very fast, because Google's office suite actually makes it easy for OpenAI to call directly — the software charging model is simple, and as long as users are still paying, Google doesn't care whether it is the top of the customer acquisition funnel.

OpenAI internally believes its biggest competitor has never been Anthropic or xAI, but Google. Google's position is too good: horizontally it has search, YouTube, and enterprise-facing workspace; vertically it extends from cloud to self-developed chips. Gemini has 650 million monthly actives, GPT over 1 billion. Google can fight a price war from two angles: first, absolute price, where TPU vertical integration lets the same model achieve higher margins; second, bundling, where a 20-dollar YouTube user can add Gemini for 10 dollars. Freda thinks the reasonable medium-to-long-term landscape is Google taking mid-to-low-end subscriptions, and GPT keeping the high-end market of several hundred or even several thousand dollars a month.

points.h: The Google threat is equally real
points.body: Freda thinks the market's negative sentiment toward OpenAI and positive sentiment toward Google is a bit too one-sided. Google's search ads haven't fallen today because everyone still uses GPT as a giant Wikipedia, asking why the sky is blue — a kind of Q&A Google never monetized anyway. But insurance and law firms are Google's biggest advertisers — buying car insurance today might mean googling and clicking the top ad slot, and that question is too suitable to ask GPT, which may already know the user drives very badly and can customize the best one. Once GPT starts doing ads and agentic commerce, the landscape will change. Total US ad revenue is only so much; if OpenAI wants to sell ads, it has to take them from Google and Meta.

points.h: The two model companies assume opposite directions
points.body: Over 80% of Anthropic's revenue is 2B, and within a year it went from losing 2 for every 1 earned to gross margins roughly comparable to OpenAI's. From 100 million to 1 billion in revenue, OpenAI took less than two quarters, Anthropic took four or five; but from 1 billion upward it reverses, with Anthropic's annualized revenue going from 1 to 7 billion in less than ten months. Freda points out an interesting divergence in the two companies' financial forecasts: Anthropic assumes total compute stops growing after 2028, and margins rise because training costs no longer grow rapidly; OpenAI assumes model ROI improves year by year, so one dollar returns five dollars the next year. So it's not that Anthropic spends less, but that it assumes a higher return rate.

points.h: Robinhood is a case of playing a bad hand well
points.body: Robinhood is the number one stock in the S&P 500 this year, but Freda says its business model is inherently poor — securities trading is highly cyclical, with heavy activity in bull markets and nothing in bear markets. It can do four things: diversify (already over 11 business lines, over 100 million in revenue), grab market share to smooth the cycle, pricing power (crypto commissions went from 10 points to 60 points in three years), and cost-side discipline (operating costs flat since 2022, a horizontal line). Freda stresses being honest with yourself about whether you're earning beta or alpha: Coinbase has had no alpha relative to Bitcoin since 2022, while Robinhood has strong alpha relative to both Bitcoin and the Nasdaq.

points.h: AI revenue must tear a hole in the labor market
points.body: Freda proposes the concept of "electronic revenue": US online advertising is about 260 billion, e-commerce commissions about 100 billion, subscriptions about 50 billion, totaling about 400 billion. If OpenAI wants to reach 200 billion in revenue entirely by grabbing existing share, then Google, Meta and Amazon all have to give up share, and burning so much money to carve out only a small pie isn't very meaningful. He thinks total advertising has no reason to increase because of AI; US companies spend an average of 3% of revenue on advertising, and there's no reason for it to exceed 3% with AI. The real space is in America's 30 trillion GDP and 15 trillion in labor costs; customer service alone is a 300 billion market, and tearing a hole there could yield hundreds of billions in revenue.

quotes.text: So it's a very simple add 2, subtract 10, and you become a -8. The large-model business model is essentially a negative snowball: every year burns more cash than the year before.
The thing you burn money on only truly generates cash flow on the day you stop burning it. That is the essence of a model company.
I think investing is quite important: you have to be honest with yourself and know what money you're earning — beta or alpha.
I think empty talk about whether it's a bubble is too subjective and maybe too hollow, but there are two levels on which you can think about this question.
